question:
A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of body aches and sore throat for 1 week. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He lives with his parents; they recently adopted a cat from an animal shelter. He is sexually active with one female partner, and they use condoms consistently. His temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 99/min, and blood pressure is 110/72 mm Hg. Examination shows bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The pharynx is red and swollen. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 15 g/dL
Leukocyte count 11,500/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 48%
Band forms 2%
Basophils 0.5%
Eosinophils 1%
Lymphocytes 45%
Monocytes 3.5%
When the patient's serum is added to a sample of horse erythrocytes, the cells aggregate together. Which of the following is the most likely causal pathogen?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Exposure to cat from animal shelter -> Possible toxoplasmosis infection -> Elevated eosinophils -> Toxoplasma gondii infection -> 70% CHAIN: Sore throat and body aches -> Pharyngitis -> Epstein-Barr virus infection -> Positive Monospot test -> Epstein-Barr virus -> 60% CHAIN: Lymphadenopathy -> Viral infection -> Epstein-Barr virus or Cytomegalovirus -> 50% CHAIN: Positive horse erythrocyte aggregation test -> Parasitic infection -> Toxoplasma gondii -> 70%
enhanced_information: The most likely causal pathogen in this case is Epstein-Barr virus, supported by the patient's symptoms of sore throat, body aches, lymphadenopathy, and positive Monospot test. The evidence of horse erythrocyte aggregation test is not directly related to Toxoplasma gondii infection in this context.
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms suggestive of infectious mononucleosis, including sore throat, body aches, lymphadenopathy, and positive Monospot test. The horse erythrocyte aggregation test is characteristic of infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The other pathogens listed are less likely based on the clinical presentation and test results.
